en: *The Moonlight of Drama*.
Homage to the illustrious Śrī Śrī Kṛṣṇacaitanya, the moon!
Having examined the scripture of the sage Bharata, which is like a beautiful moon filled with the nectar of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), [this work is composed].
This definition of drama is written here in extreme brevity.
Because it is not very well-connected and because it contradicts the opinion of the sage Bharata,
the method [of analysis] found in the Sāhityadarpaṇa has generally not been adopted here.
It is endowed with the divine, the both-divine-and-non-divine, and likewise the non-divine;
it is enriched by the steadfast, the exalted, the dark, and the graceful.
In a delightful [drama], where one of the sentiments of love (śṛṅgāra) or heroism (vīra) is predominant and which possesses uninterrupted continuity,
there should be a connection at the end of the prologue (prastāvanā), integrated with the junctures (sandhi) and their constituent parts (sandhyaṅga).
It is endowed with twenty-one internal junctures (*sandhi*), adorned with thirty-six ornaments,
and likewise provided with the positions of the banners (*patākā-sthānaka*) as well as the gestures of indifference (*upekṣepaka*).
This drama is endowed with the rules of linguistic expression, filled with the qualities of excellent poetry,
free from defects, and bestows all-encompassing bliss.
In that regard, the protagonist is said to be divine, such as Kṛṣṇa and others, whose sovereignty is self-manifested.
However, because he exhibits human behavior despite being divine, the scion of Raghu (Rāma) is considered both divine and non-divine.
Among these, Kṛṣṇa—who is not a divine being like the "Dharma-sons" and others—is superior in qualities;
for in him all the various types of qualities belonging to heroes are traditionally held to reside.
In this [hero], the abundance of beauty is even greater than that of grace and audacity;
therefore, he is the hero appropriate for a drama dominated by the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).

As for what has been stated by the wise regarding the secondary nature of [the relationship] with another's wife or son—that indeed applies to everyone except Kṛṣṇa and the gopīs; so it has been established.

And so it has been said in the *Rasavilāsa* (composed by Sudeva): "That [the sentiment of love] is not desired by poets for any other principal sentiment (*aṅgin*) except when it belongs to the family of those with eyes like lotuses from Gokula."
Out of a desire for the composition of this aesthetic essence,
it was introduced by the Enemy of Kaṃsa, the crest-jewel of the circle of connoisseurs.

Now, regarding the aesthetic sentiments (rasas): the sentiments such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra) and the heroic (vīra) are to be understood in this ocean of the nectar of rasa; other sentiments, such as the comic (hāsya) and so forth, should be employed by the wise as subordinate elements within it.
Now, regarding the plot (itivṛtta): the plot is of three kinds—well-known (khyāta), invented (kalpita), and mixed (miśra).
That which is well-known is established in the scriptures; that which is invented is composed by the poet.
The mingling of these two is called *saṅkula*; however, that which is composed [of such elements] is beautiful in a *nāṭaka*.
A *nāṭaka* should have a well-known plot, whereas a *nāṭikā* has a composed plot.
An *īhāmṛga* has a mixed plot; thus it is stated in the *Nāṭyāṅga*.

Now, the introduction: next, the source (tīrtha) for this subject matter to be established is stated as the introduction (prastāvanā). At the beginning of the introduction, however, an auspicious benediction (nāndī) should be performed.
It is endowed with one of the three— benediction, salutation, or statement of the subject—
and is composed of eight, ten, or twelve words.
It is generally marked with the name of the moon, radiant with words of auspicious meaning;
and its auspicious symbols include the wheel, the lotus, the ruddy goose, the night-lily, and so forth.
Among these, that which is accompanied by a benediction (*āśīr-anvitā*) is as follows, in the *Lalitamādhava* (1.1):
"The breasts of the women who are the enemies of the gods [are like] ruddy geese..."
May the moon of Mukunda’s glory— the friend of all, the delighter of the cakora birds, and the one whose rays cause the lotus-faces [of his devotees] to blossom— grant you joy for a long time.
Accompanied by an act of homage,
as it is said in that very same work (1.2):
"Having sprinkled the eight quarters with thick juices, [he beheld] the splendor of the young shoots."

We bow down here to that dark cloud-like Kṛṣṇa, who, while constantly adorning the rows of beautiful women with a profusion of loveliness, strides forth while covering the daughter of the Sun on his broad chest— she who possesses incomparable luster and a moon-like form.
And here, the *vastu-nirdeśa* (indication of the subject matter) is likewise [contained] in the verse beginning with "Having sprinkled the eight quarters," and so forth.
An example of one joined with eight *padas* is found in the first act of the *Vīracarita* (the first verse of the prologue): [text follows].
Salutation to the internal, pure, eternal God, who has removed all evil,
who has abandoned sequential divisions, and whose nature is the light of consciousness.
Someone sang an eight-pada verse with eight feet in two lines.
It is endowed with ten feet, as in the *Abhirāmarāghava*:
"The glances of [Viṣṇu], who has risen from his serpent-bed, are auspicious in their actions; they are waves in the stream of the essence of the flow of compassion."
These [words] are friends to the auspicious fortune of the petals of the play-lotus of Hari's Lakṣmī;
they bloom with the essence of nectar and are easily obtained only through the excellence of virtuous conduct.
As in the verse beginning, "The breasts of the fair-eyed wives of the enemies of the gods," which consists of twelve feet;
here too, there is the auspiciousness marked by the name of the Moon. This four-lined meter is appropriate for the Goddess of Speech.
And likewise, *prarocanā* occurs at the beginning of the *vīthī* and the *prahasana*.
In that context, *prarocanā* (the incitement to interest) is defined as follows:

it is the act of turning the listeners' attention toward the discourse by means of praising the place, the time, the story, the teacher, the assembly, and so forth; this is what is called *prarocanā*.
As in the *Lalitamādhava* (1.7): the Director says,
"Why is it said thus?"
Look, look!
The festival of autumn shines forth; the assembly of Vaiṣṇavas sparkles;
and after a long time, the mountain pours forth a stream of pure fame for Hari.
What else is this that the sweet-formed Mādhava shines forth here?
It is surely the supreme excellence resulting from the glory of your pure merit.
Now, the prologue (āmukha): when the stage manager (sūtradhāra) speaks to the actress (naṭī) regarding his own business by means of artifice,
using striking speech that introduces the subject at hand, that is called the prologue (āmukha).
That which is called the "introduction" (āmukha) is itself also termed the "prologue" (prastāvanā).
The five components of the introduction are said to be: the narrative prelude (kathodghāta) and the inciting agent (pravartaka).
And the excellence of application; thus the sage has declared the pair of limbs belonging to the *vīthī*: the *udghātyaka* and the *avalagita*.
In that regard, the "Opening of the Narrative" (kathodghāta) is defined as follows:
When an actor enters by adopting either the words of the author or the meaning thereof, in accordance with his own character's history, that is celebrated as the Opening of the Narrative. (RNc 23)
As it is said in the *Harivilāsa*:
"Who is able to know the heart of those whose burden of greatness is incomparable, whose intentions are difficult for the world to comprehend, and whose conduct transcends that of ordinary men?"
(Offstage) Ah, indeed! You have spoken the truth: who is able to know the heart of those whose conduct is superhuman?
Now, regarding the instigator (pravartaka):
"The instigator would be that which, having been projected by the equality of time, brings about activity. (RN 24)
As it is said in the *Keśavacarita*:
"Causing the multitude of flowers to bloom all around,
and instantly increasing the splendor of Uddhava..."
O beautiful one, this Mādhava, who intoxicates even the minds of the wise and brings joy on all sides, has now met you.
Thus they both exit. Then Mādhava enters.
As it is said in the *Vidagdhamādhava* (1.10):
"This very spring season has arrived, in which..."

On the night of the full moon, that full moon itself shall bring together for the sake of amorous play that Lord— who is filled with fresh, newly arrived attendants— and Rādhā, who is beautiful with her hidden passion.

Now, the *prayogātiśaya* (the excellence of performance): "When there is an indication of an entrance through the performance of the *sūtradhāra* by means of an introductory remark such as 'This is he,' that indeed is *prayogātiśaya*. (RN 25)
As it says in the *Lalitā-Mādhava*, in the fourth act of the *Garbha* section:
"This Mādhava always delights Rādhikā perfectly and without hindrance, even though she is constantly being obstructed by her elder [Yashodā]."
Now, the *udghātyaka*:
when words whose meaning is not yet understood are joined by people with other words for the sake of reaching that meaning, it is called *udghātyaka*.
As it is said in the *Lalitā-Mādhava* (1.11):
"Having slain the King of the Kirātas while acting as a dancer on the stage, that treasury of arts must now, at the proper time, perform the seizing of Tārā’s hand, O virtuous lady."

(Offstage) Ah! Unable to openly proclaim the marriage of Rādhā and Mādhava for fear of King Kaṃsa, who is this fortunate man who, by acting as a Kirāta king and instructing me with such counsel, comforts me as I am overwhelmed with anxiety? Here enters Paurṇamāsī.
Now, *avagalita* (the slipped):
where, having undertaken one task, another is accomplished by way of compliance with what preceded; that should be known as *avagalita* by the wise. (RNc 27)
As in the *Kaṃsavadha*:
"O Puruṣottama, King of Dancers, why do you delay? (Offstage) "Ho! Who are you that you urge me to hurry here?"
The Director: How is it that the Blessed One, in the guise of a cowherd, has actually arrived? Look, look!
And so forth.
In a drama abounding in the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), the prologue (āmukha) alone is appropriate;
for neither the vīthī nor the prahasana is observed here [in such a context].
Therefore, in the *Lalitavistara* (Lalita-mādhave), there is an *āmukha*;
some clearly state that the *prastāvanā* and *sthāpanā* are two other divisions of the *āmukha*,
and they provide the definitions for those two.
For example,
the prologue (prastāvanāmukha) should consist of a dialogue between the actress, the buffoon, and the actor, combined with a brief introductory scene (vīthī) and so forth.
That very [performance], together with all the processional avenues and so forth, is called "establishment" (sthāpanā).
In most cases involving heroes, wonders, and the like, the "introduction" (prastāvanā) is appropriate.
In the cases of the comic, the loathsome, the furious, and so forth, it is generally held that there is a fixed [sentiment];
however, the *vīthī* and the *prahasana* are remembered as two distinct varieties among the dramatic forms (*rūpaka*).
Now, regarding *sandhi* (transition):
the union of each individual state with one fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) at a time is to be known as *sandhi* by those proficient in the science of drama.
In that regard, the *prakṛti* (the basic elements):
"Because the narrative consists of five parts, its *prakṛti* is traditionally held to be fivefold:
the seed (*bīja*), the drop (*bindu*), the banner (*patākā*), the minor incident (*prakarī*), and the main action (*kārya*) itself. (RNc 31)
In this context, the seed (bīja) is that which, though cast forth in a very small measure, undergoes expansion in many ways;
it is called the "seed" by the wise because it is the cause of the effect.

Just as in the *Lalitamādhava*, where the seed (*bīja*) is said to be the established passion (*anurāga*) of Rādhā and Mādhava, conceived within the opening juncture (*mukha-sandhi*) of the first and second acts;
now, the "drop" (*bindu*):
When the primary fruit of a seed has been interrupted by other incidental fruits mentioned in the context,
that which serves as the cause for its non-interruption is called the *bindu*.

Just as in that same place, in the third and fourth *pratimukha-sandhi*s, when the primary fruit [of union] was interrupted by the departure for Kṛṣṇa’s city and so forth, there arose a hope for that very fruit through the words of Sūrya heard in the water, beginning with: "Take these [maidens] quickly; how many are there? and so on, which generated an expectation of Kṛṣṇa.
By the statement beginning with "maṅkṣu-mimaṅkṣum" (4.10), the *bindu* is the embryo (*garbha*). Now, the *patākā*:

That which is an accessory to the primary subject matter and, by way of incidental connection, attains its own purpose, is called a "banner" (patākā) by the wise, as in the story of the minister of the Yadavas.

Just as in that same work, in the fifth and sixth acts, the events concerning the full moon and Uddhava at the imagined junction of the womb constitute the *patākā* (the secondary incident); now follows the *prakarī* (the minor incident):
That which accomplishes solely the welfare of others and pertains to a specific location is designated as a *prakarī*, like the conduct of the nine groups (*navavṛnda*) and so forth.
Just as in that very same [work], in the seventh and eighth chapters, within the imagined juncture of contemplation (*vimarṣa-sandhi*),
there is the *prakarī* consisting of the conduct of the nine groups (*nava-vṛnda*) and so forth, and the clans (*kula*) and so forth.
Now, as for the *kārya* (the effect): it is traditionally held that the *kārya* is that which is to be accomplished by the entire subject matter,
such as the union of Rādhā and Mādhava in the *Lalitamādhava*.
Just as here, in the ninth and tenth [cantos], within the *nirvahaṇa* juncture (*sandhi*) which is conceived [as such], there is the sport and so forth of Rādhā and Mādhava preceded by their reunion.
Furthermore, that which consists of the primary element and its subordinate elements is of two kinds:
the primary is the life-story of the Leader, while the pervasive is the activity of Kṛṣṇa.

The *kṛtāṅga* (accomplished act) serves the purpose of the hero (*nāyaka*), while the activities of those other than the hero constitute the *patākā* (ensign) and *prakarī* (episode); these are always constituent parts (*aṅga*), whereas the *bīja* (seed) and so forth occur only occasionally.
Because it is the seed, the seed should be at the beginning; because it is the fruit, the effect should be at the end.
Because it is the cause of their conjunction, one should repeatedly insert the *bindu* in between them.
The banners and the various ornaments should be arranged according to their appropriate positions.
Therefore, the *bindu* is like that described in the fifth [chapter] (LalM 5.23): "The dark blue of Hari, deeper than a fresh *tāmāla* tree, surpassing a stream of shimmering jewels."
Victorious is his charming chest, upon which fresh saffron has been applied;
it always resembles a cloud that, blossoming with clusters of stars and bearing a weight of splendor intensified by lightning, shines forth playfully and boundlessly.
In this same way, the bindu should also be observed in the sixth, seventh, and subsequent [syllables].
Now, as for the stages: the fivefold stage of the action [of the plot] arises through the agency of the protagonist and others;
these are inception, effort, attainment, hope, and the arrival of the certain fruit. (RNc 41)
In that context, "commencement" (ārambha) is defined by the wise as the exertion toward the primary fruit;
for example, in the *Mukhasandhi* of the *Lalitamādhava*, it is the effort of Rādhā and Mādhava toward their mutual union.
Determination is the undertaking; now, as for effort— effort,
however, is the engagement with zeal toward the attainment of its fruit.
Just as in that very same *pratimukha-sandhi*, while Rādhā was searching for Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa made an effort—
an exertion— to be seen by Rādhā during the dance performed by the Gandharvas and other events;
this is then followed by the hope of attainment (*prāpty-āśā*).
The hope for attainment, however, is considered the possibility of accomplishing one's own goal.
[*NOTE: The cultivation of the perfected state is considered [the means].
And likewise, it was said by the Sage (19.11): "When some slight attainment of the fruit is conceived,"
Those who know the rules declare that its attainment is possible through mere intention alone.

For example, in that very same embryonic juncture (*garbha-sandhi*), there is the hope for attainment (*prāptyāśā*) because Kṛṣṇa’s entrusting of Rādhā to Satrājit and His acquisition of Lalitā, Śaṅkhacūḍa, the jewel, and so forth, render Him worthy of being honored.
Now, the certain attainment (*niyatāpti*):

Attainment of certainty (*niyatāpti*) is the conviction regarding the successful accomplishment of the task without obstacle. For example, in that same *vimarśa* juncture, because of the sight of Rādhā, there is the attainment of certainty due to the conviction in the successful accomplishment of the fruit without obstacle.
Now, regarding the attainment of the fruit: the attainment of one's own desired fruit is indeed what constitutes the attainment of the fruit (phalāgama).
Just as in that very same *nirvahaṇa* juncture,
there is the attainment of the fruit, such as the reunion with the Friend of Vraja, the gaining of Rādhā, and the consecration with jewels;
however, the presence of the *patākā* (the secondary plot) may exist in some cases, or it may not exist at all.
But when it is devoid of the banner, one should place the seed-syllable and the bindu.

Now, the components of the juncture (sandhy-aṅgāni): When there is a connection of the subsidiary parts of the narrative by virtue of the primary purpose, the relation of intermediate meanings is the "juncture" (sandhi), which takes the form of a joining (sandhāna). (RNc 45)

The Mukha (Opening), Pratimukha (Progression), Garbha (Development), Vimarśa (Crisis), and Upasaṃhṛti (Conclusion)—these are the five junctures (*saṃdhi*). Among them, the definition of the Mukha is stated: [RNc 46]
Now, regarding the "mouth" (mukha):
the mouth is the emergence of the seed, from which various meanings and aesthetic sentiments arise;
herein, however, there are twelve limbs, in accordance with the commencement of that seed.
Here, the emergence of the seed of love between Rādhā and Mādhava is indicated by its excellence,
as it was [previously] shown in the *Lalita-mādhava*.
Introduction, elaboration, conclusion, enticement,
application, attainment, resolution, arrangement, and contemplation.
The definitions of their unfolding (*udbheda*), division (*bheda*), and means of execution (*karaṇa*) are now stated.
Among these, the "introduction" (*upakṣepa*)—the introduction is said by the wise to be the indication of the seed (*bīja*). (RN 50)
As in the first act of the *Lalitā-Mādhava* (1.14), Paurṇamāsī says— (having read "Alas, regarding Rādhā and Mādhava!")— "Child Gārgī, listen."
Having drunk the nectar within the city of Rādhā’s smile-moonlight river— where the Yamunā and Gaṅgā have been merged into a single braid by the waves of Kṛṣṇa’s dark-cornered eyes—
their heaps of suffering are devoured by the intensely swelling frost of inner satisfaction.
Having traversed the seven worlds, we now abide at the very summit of all.
Here, the indication of the seed of the passion between Rādhā and Mādhava is the *upakṣepa* (the introductory hint).
Now, as for the *parikara* (the elaboration): "The expansion of the seed [plot] is to be known by the wise as the *parikara*."
As it is said in that very same place (1.24):
"Gārgī, who is skillful, seizes Rādhā by the garment and drags her from the house to the forest."
Victorious is that female messenger, born of a noble lineage, who possesses a sweet, low-pitched voice and has been entrusted with full authority.
In this case, because the seed of passion is made to flourish through such means as drawing [the lover] into the forest, it is the *parikara* (preparation).
Now, regarding the secondary assignment (parinyāsa): the exposition of the production of the seed-syllables is called the secondary assignment.
As it says in that very same first act— Rādhā (with horripilation): "Lalita, who indeed is being heard of, since [the news] reaches only the ear?"
I am being driven to madness by this constant longing.
[Lalita, who indeed is this one called Kṛṣṇa,
by whose mere becoming a guest to my ears I am thus driven to madness?]
In this context, *parinyāsa* (the final placement) consists in the description of the production of the seed (*bīja*) by means of causing intoxication.
Now, as for *vilobhana* (enticement): it is the description of the qualities of the hero and other characters; that is *vilobhana*.
As it occurs in that very same first act: there Kṛṣṇa (approaching) beholds your radiant orb of a face, O Rādhikā.
With a mind overwhelmed by a weight of shame,

the moon— evidently wishing to attain a splendor equal to his— is performing austerities, having grown thin and taken refuge in the forest of Śiva’s clearly visible matted locks, which are moistened by the waves of the celestial river.

In that regard, there is seduction through the description of Rādhā’s beauty and virtues. Now, as for the application (*yukti*): "The thorough determination of the purposes is indeed intended as the application. (RNc 54)
As it says in that very same place (Para 1.111–2):
Yaśodā says— “Bhadrī, Candrāvalī, Nomālikā, Rādhā, Māhārī, and all of you fulfill all my hopes with a flood of the splendor of your virtues.”
There too, like a bee taking a flower,
he delights with the nectar of his beauty the bee-like eyes.
O Blessed One, Candrāvalī, Navamālikā, Rādhā, and Mādhavī completely fulfill my hope with a flood of the fragrance of their virtues;
even among them, the young girl is like a dear calf to me.
The slender one delights the bee of the eye with the nectar of her beauty. The Blessed One said: "O Gokuleśvarī, such indeed is the conduct of all the inhabitants of Gokula."
In this context, *yukti* (reasoning) is the determination of Rādhā’s excellence of qualities as being superior in every respect.
Now, *prāpti* (attainment): the attainment of happiness by the wise is designated as *prāpti*.
As it is said in that very same place (1.51):
"There, Kṛṣṇa— again becoming attentive with his ears pricked up and his hair standing on end— [is he who] with waves of sweetness causes [the world] to freeze in the sky."
The cries of the cranes, fresh with the intoxication of passion,
arise in my heart as the tinkling of Rādhā’s girdle, transforming them into a grand display of amorous agitation.
In this context, the attainment of bliss by Kṛṣṇa upon hearing Rādhā’s humming is "attainment" (prāpti).
Now, as for "re-establishment" (samādhāna): the re-establishment of the seed is here called "re-establishment."
As it is said in that very same place—
Rādhā (tearfully):
"O Kuṇḍalā, will you indeed even dig a path for this one wretched man?"
O Kuṇḍalatā,
will she perhaps even for a moment set foot upon the path of that one wretched-eyed man, my fortunate Kanna?
"Karṇa is the guest.
Here, there is a resolution (*samādhāna*) because Rādhā herself has once again sown the seed of passion.
Now, the arrangement (*vidhāna*):
The wise know that which produces pleasure and pain to be the "ordinance" (vidhāna).
As it occurs in that very same second act—
Rādhikā: (gazing slightly at Kṛṣṇa from a distance,
aside in Sanskrit)
"O companion, who is this fearless youth, possessing the luster of a rain-cloud and the grace of a rutting elephant, who has arrived here from where in the land of Vraja?
Alas! With his flickering side-glances that steal away [the heart], they surge upward."
"He who here plunders my resolve and the wealth of my mind from the treasury of my heart.
(2.11) (Looking again) Alas, alas! A great mistake!
Lalita, look, look! Having seen this Brahmacārin, my heart is deeply agitated;
therefore, for this great sinner, entry into the fire is the only [remedy].
The mind of another:
[Alas, woe! Woe! What negligence!
O Lalitā, look, look at this!]
"Having seen this celibate student, my heart has been pierced and destroyed.
Therefore, for this great sin,
entry into the fire alone is the atonement."
Lalitā: Friend, you speak the truth!
Therefore, she must surely be concealing her omniscience.
[“Friend, you speak the truth; surely it is the similarity of our complexions that causes this delusion.
Rādhikā: (Looking again,)
O companion, this Hari has assumed the guise of Brahmā;
otherwise, why would my inner self flee from him?
"The moonstone pedestal does not, indeed, produce a stream of perspiration without the moonlight of the lord of night-lotuses.
(2.12) Here, there is *vidhāna* because of the description of pleasure and pain arising from Rādhā’s perception of Kṛṣṇa and her perception of a brahmin.
Now, regarding cultivation (paribhāvanā):
Cultivation is the wonder of the mind produced by a flood of praiseworthy virtues.
As it occurs in that very same first act—
Rādhā (with astonishment, in Sanskrit):
"Shattering the masses of stones that are the virtues of noble-born maidens..."

O fair-faced one, who is this unprecedented Viśvakarman before us, who simultaneously sweeps the courtyard with hundreds of thousands of emerald jewels using the strokes of his sharp, long-cornered chisels? 52.
Lalitā: Friend,
there he is, your lord of life!
Rādhā: (In a state of madness, again in Sanskrit) Is this indeed that moon who is the nectar-rayed luminary for the night-lotuses of the cowherd girls?
Is this indeed that festival of the installation of the crown prince shining upon Gokula?

O slender-waisted one, does he— who is a flower-garden for the diversion of my mind and heart— sprinkle this pair of eyes with waves of nectar? (1.53) Here, by means of the illustration of Kṛṣṇa’s qualities such as cleverness and beauty, [the state of being overwhelmed by love is shown].
From the narration of Rādhā’s marvel arises *paribhāvanā*.
Now, *udbheda*: the emergence of the seed is known as *udbheda*. (RNc 59)
As in that very same second act—
Rādhikā (aside, in Sanskrit):
As long as fear flashes within from the heavy gaze of the fickle-eyed one, my sense of family honor remains fully manifest in my mind;
[yet I behold her] with cheeks blooming and shimmering with moving shark-shaped earrings.

"As long as this lotus-face of the speaker does not depart from direct perception. (2.26) Here, at the outset, because the seed of passion that had been concealed is disclosed by her own mouth, there is *udbheda* (manifestation).
Now, *bheda* (separation).
The stimulation of the seed is its differentiation, or else it is the breaking apart of the aggregate.
As it is said in that very same place:
Kundalatā says, "O Rāhu,
your splendor is unshakable."
Therefore, enough with proclaiming it yourself. [Rādhā, I know that your vow of chastity has faltered; so, enough with proclaiming it yourself.]
Viśākhā— (With affectionate indignation) Kuṇḍalā, who else indeed but you is being summoned by Vaṃśī three times a day?
"O Rādhā, what other woman of your lineage indeed is drawn [to the flute] at the three junctions of the day like you?
(Kundalatā, with a playful smile)
